sentences: A young woman stands behind the marble bar at the Folies-Bergère, one of the most glittering music halls in Paris.
At the centre of the canvas, she alone looks quietly back at us.
All around is noise; her face is perfectly still.
Édouard Manet showed this painting at the Paris Salon of 1882.
He made sketches on site, then set up a bar in his studio and painted the whole picture there.
The model was Suzon, a real barmaid at the Folies-Bergère, who came to pose for him.
Let's look closely at her face.
Beneath her fringe, she gazes ahead with an expression that gives nothing away.
She neither smiles nor speaks, and the Courtauld calls her the still centre of the painting.
The chandeliers and the crowded balcony behind her are all a reflection in a huge mirror.
That means the noisy room is really on our side of the bar.
Loose, rapid brushwork turns the crowd into a kind of glittering hum.
Look into the top left corner.
A pair of feet in green boots dangles into view.
They belong to a trapeze artist performing above the audience.
With just these two feet, Manet hints at the whole show happening out of frame.
Now come down to the bottles on the left of the counter.
There is gold-foiled champagne, and bottles of English beer marked with a red triangle.
On the label of the bottle at the far left, Manet signed his name and the date, 1882.
Move your eyes to the right, and you will find a glass bowl heaped with oranges and two flowers in a tumbler.
Cool marble and glass meet the warm glow of fruit, and the still life could stand as a painting on its own.
Now look to the upper right.
Her reflected back has slipped far off to the right, where she seems to face a male customer in a top hat.
Yet in front of the woman we see head-on, there is no such man.
That misplaced reflection has been argued over ever since the picture was first shown in 1882.
The Courtauld explains that Manet ignored normal perspective and shifted it to the right.
In 2000, one art historian staged a reconstruction showing the view was physically possible.
It was Manet's last major painting, finished a year before he died in 1883.
After his death the composer Emmanuel Chabrier bought it and hung it over his piano.
Samuel Courtauld acquired it in 1926, and it now hangs at the Courtauld Gallery in London.
Step back and let your eyes move between her face and her reflection.
In the middle of this noisy night, what might she be thinking?
And are we, perhaps, standing exactly where that gentleman stands?
